# Weekly Book Topics 50Q - week of 6 Sep 2026 (Mon 7 - Sat 12 Sep)

*Auto-generated for UPSC CSE 2027 prep. Feeds the website's Sectional practice flow. Static book-topic set, not current affairs.*

## Week focus

**Basis:** the **Sunday Sweep dated 2026-09-06**, which plans **Sun 6 Sep -> Sat 12 Sep 2026**. That Sweep introduces a structural change - **Sunday is now revision-only**, so all new reading is compressed into **Mon 7 - Sat 12 Sep**, which is the **first half of F8** (8-21 Sep). This set therefore tests the six days of new material, not Sunday.

The Sweep's own Sunday row asks for the Book-topics 50Q to be run "against **Laxmikanth Ch 45 (Governor)** - but as a *pre-read diagnostic* for tomorrow, not as new study: attempt it cold, mark what you don't know, and let Monday's reading answer it." The set is weighted accordingly, and then covers the rest of the week's static reading in proportion to the hours the Sweep allots it.

| Block | Source | Q | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Polity - State Government** | Laxmikanth **Ch 45-49**: Governor, Chief Minister, State Council of Ministers, State Legislature, Special Provisions | Q1-15 | The week's anchor and the largest single allocation in the Sweep - five chapters across Mon, Thu, Fri and Sat. Articles 153-167, 200-201, 213, 164(1A)/(1B), 169-171, and the whole of Part XXI. |
| **Economy - Infrastructure + Land Reforms** | Vivek Singh **Ch 14** (the F7 carry-over) **+ Ch 5** | Q16-23 | Tuesday's double block. Four on the PPP model ladder and infrastructure financing, four on the land-reform legs. Economy is studied from **NCERT + Vivek Singh, not Mrunal**. |
| **Ancient History - Mahajanapadas to the Mauryas** | TN State Board Class 11 | Q24-31 | Wednesday's two-hour continuous narrative, and only the **second** Ancient reading of the cycle. The Sweep names Ancient as the thinnest area in the corpus, so it is deliberately over-weighted relative to its two hours. |
| **Environment - Waste + Climate Change** | Shankar IAS **Ch 7-8** | Q32-38 | Thursday's first half. The waste-stream rules ladder and the UNFCCC -> Kyoto -> Paris architecture, plus India's NDC. |

The questions exploit that pairing. |

**No repeats.** The last six book-topics sets (26 Jul, 02 Aug x2, 09 Aug x2, 11 Aug, 16 Aug, 23 Aug, 30 Aug) closed Polity through the **Union** institutions and the constitutional bodies (Laxmikanth Ch 10-44), Vivek Singh through Ch 13, Spectrum through the British-rule thematics, physical and human Geography (NCERT-11 complete, NCERT-12 Ch 1-5), Shankar Ch 3-6, space / nuclear / defence / biotechnology, and IR with the US, China and Russia files. **Nothing here repeats any of them.** Three areas are entering the corpus for the first time: **the State Government block** (last week was the *Union* judiciary and the constitutional bodies - this week is a level down and is written around the contrast), **Land Reforms**, and **Art & Culture**, which has never appeared in a book-topics set. Ancient History appeared once, on 30 Aug, covering Indus and Vedic only; this set advances to the Mahajanapadas and the Mauryas with no overlap. This is a clean advance, not a revision round.

**Verification note.** Two moving items were web-checked before use rather than written from memory, because both had changed:

- **Q7** rests on the Supreme Court's **advisory opinion of 20 November 2025** in the Presidential Reference on Articles 200 and 201, which held that courts cannot impose timelines on the Governor or the President, that there is no 'deemed assent', and that these decisions are not ordinarily justiciable - while preserving **limited** review where a Governor simply does not act. This **supersedes** the timelines laid down in *State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu* (April 2025), which the opinion described as erroneous. The Sweep's Monday note warns against writing "a settled-law sentence you will have to unlearn"; the position is now settled, and this is what it settled to.
- **Q50** uses the **Ganga Waters Treaty**, signed 12 December 1996 for a term of thirty years and **due to expire on 31 December 2026**, with renewal discussions under way. Dry-season sharing at Farakka: below 70,000 cusecs the flow is shared equally.

Nothing here is claimed to be a verbatim UPSC PYQ. The stems follow UPSC's statement-based, pair-matching, chronology and single-best-answer patterns, but all fifty are newly written.

## How to use

**Sunday evening, 18:00-19:00, cold and closed-book, in one 60-minute sitting** - as the Sweep specifies, this is a **pre-read diagnostic**, not a test of work already done. You have not read Laxmikanth Ch 45-49 yet. You are *supposed* to drop marks on Q1-15. Mark and move; do not linger.

Then do only one thing with the result: **mark every question you could not place, and take that list into Monday's reading.** Do not look up the answers first. Read Ch 45 with the list beside you and let the chapter answer it - a question you have already failed at, answered from the book eighteen hours later, sets far harder than a question you got right by luck.

The rest of the set works the other way. Q24-50 cover material also unread, but Q16-23 (Economy) and Q32-38 (Environment) sit closer to what you already know from Vivek Singh Ch 10-13 and Shankar Ch 5-6. Treat a miss there as a genuine gap, not a diagnostic.

**Benchmark:** because this is a cold pre-read, the usual Easy-set benchmark does not apply on the Polity block. Apply it to Q32-50 only - more than three dropped among the Easy questions there means the earlier Environment and Geography chapters have decayed, and that is a spaced-repetition problem, not a new-reading problem. Difficulty mix is **15 Easy / 25 Moderate / 10 Hard**. **Re-take blind on Saturday 12 Sep**, after all six days of reading are done; the gap between the two scores is the honest measure of the week.

## Questions

**Q1.** With reference to the office of the Governor of a State, consider the following statements:
1. Article 153 provides that there shall be a Governor for each State.
2. The same person may be appointed as Governor for two or more States.
3. The Governor is elected by the members of the State Legislative Assembly.
Which of the statements given above are correct?

- (a) 1 and 2 only
- (b) 2 and 3 only
- (c) 1 and 3 only
- (d) 1, 2 and 3


**Q2.** Which one of the following correctly describes the tenure of a Governor?

- (a) He has a fixed term of five years and can be removed only by impeachment by Parliament
- (b) He holds office during the pleasure of the Prime Minister
- (c) He holds office during the pleasure of the President, with a normal term of five years
- (d) He has a term of five years and may be removed by a resolution of the State Legislative Assembly


**Q3.** Consider the following statements in respect of the office of Governor:
1. He must be a citizen of India and must have completed 35 years of age.
2. He must not be a member of Parliament or of a State legislature; if he is, he is deemed to have vacated that seat on entering office.
3. His emoluments and allowances are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?

- (a) 1 only
- (b) 1 and 2 only
- (c) 2 and 3 only
- (d) 1, 2 and 3


**Q4.** The pardoning power of the Governor under Article 161 differs from that of the President under Article 72 in that the Governor cannot:
1. pardon a sentence of death.
2. deal with a sentence passed by a court-martial.
3. remit a sentence for an offence against a law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the State extends.
Which of the statements given above are correct?

- (a) 1 only

- (c) 2 and 3 only
- (d) 1, 2 and 3


**Q5.** With reference to Article 163 of the Constitution, consider the following statements:

**Q6.** Under Article 200, when a Bill passed by the State Legislature is presented to the Governor, which of the following are correct?

## Answer key with explanations

**Q1. Answer: (a)** - *Easy* - Article 153 provides a Governor for each State; the proviso added by the Seventh Amendment Act, 1956 allows the same person to be appointed Governor of two or more States. Statement 3 is wrong: under Article 155 the Governor is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal. The Constituent Assembly considered and deliberately rejected an elected Governor, because an elected Governor with an independent mandate would rival the Chief Minister.

**Q2. Answer: (c)** - *Easy* - Article 156: the Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President and, subject to that, for a term of five years; he may resign by writing addressed to the President. There is no impeachment procedure for a Governor. In B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010) the Supreme Court held that removal need not be for cause, but cannot be arbitrary, capricious or for reasons extraneous, and is open to limited judicial review.

**Q3. Answer: (b)** - *Easy* - Article 157 lays down only two qualifications - citizenship of India and 35 years of age. Everything else (that he be an outsider to the State, that the Chief Minister be consulted) is convention, not law. Article 158 bars membership of a legislature and any office of profit. Statement 3 is wrong: under Article 158(3) his emoluments are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the STATE, and cannot be diminished during his term.

**Q4. Answer: (b)** - *Moderate* - Two exclusions separate Article 161 from Article 72: the Governor cannot pardon a death sentence, and he has no power over court-martial sentences. Statement 3 is the Governor's core power, not an exclusion - Article 161 extends precisely to offences against laws relating to matters to which the State's executive power extends. Note the trap: the Governor CAN suspend, remit or commute a death sentence under Section 473 of the BNSS (formerly Section 432 CrPC); what he cannot do is grant a PARDON for it.

**Q5. Answer: (d)** - *Moderate* - All three are correct - 163(1) carries the discretion exception, and 163(2) makes the Governor the judge of what is discretionary and shields that determination from challenge on that ground. This is the textual reason the Governor's discretion is wider than the President's: Article 74(1), after the 42nd and 44th Amendments, binds the President to ministerial advice with no corresponding discretion clause. Article 163(2) does not, however, immunise the substantive decision itself from every form of review.

**Q6. Answer: (c)** - *Moderate* - The second proviso to Article 200 makes reservation MANDATORY where the Bill would, if it became law, so derogate from the powers of the High Court as to endanger its constitutional position. The first proviso allows the Governor to return a Bill for reconsideration - but expressly NOT a Money Bill, so statement 2 is wrong - and provides that if the House passes it again, with or without amendment, the Governor shall not withhold assent.

**Q7. Answer: (d)** - *Hard* - A five-judge Constitution Bench (advisory opinion of 20 November 2025) held that the timelines read into Articles 200 and 201 in State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu (2025) were erroneous, that there is no 'deemed assent', and that the assent decision is not ordinarily justiciable. Statement 3 overstates it: the Court expressly preserved LIMITED judicial review where a Governor simply chooses not to act and thereby frustrates the legislative process, in which case a court may issue a limited direction to act - without commenting on the merits. Note this opinion also held the Governor has three options, not four, and that a reconsidered Bill may still be reserved for the President.

**Q8. Answer: (b)** - *Hard* - Article 213(1) provisos list exactly three cases requiring the President's instructions - the three in statements 1 to 3. Statement 4 is a distractor: subject-matter in the Concurrent List by itself triggers no such requirement. Remember also that the Governor's ordinance power, unlike the President's, cannot be exercised at all without instructions in those three cases, and that an ordinance must be laid before the legislature and expires six weeks after reassembly.

**Q9. Answer: (c)** - *Easy* - Article 164(1): the Chief Minister is appointed by the Governor and the other Ministers are appointed by the Governor on the Chief Minister's advice. Statement 3 is wrong - Article 164(2) makes the Council collectively responsible to the LEGISLATIVE ASSEMBLY alone, even in the six bicameral States. This is the exact parallel of the Union position, where responsibility runs to the Lok Sabha and not to the Rajya Sabha.

**Q10. Answer: (a)** - *Moderate* - Article 164(1A), inserted by the 91st Amendment, 2003: 15% of the Legislative Assembly's total strength, with a FLOOR of 12. Option (d) is the trap - it states the Union position under Article 75(1A), which caps the Union Council at 15% of the Lok Sabha's strength with no floor. The same amendment inserted Article 164(1B): a member disqualified on the ground of defection is also disqualified from being appointed a Minister.

**Q11. Answer: (b)** - *Moderate* - The proviso to Article 164(1) names four States - Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha - where there shall be a Minister in charge of tribal welfare, who may in addition be in charge of the welfare of the Scheduled Castes and backward classes or any other work. Bihar was in the original list; Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand were added by the Madhya Pradesh and Bihar Reorganisation Acts of 2000, and Bihar was subsequently dropped. Rajasthan has never been in the list.

**Q12. Answer: (a)** - *Moderate* - Article 169: Parliament may by ordinary law abolish or create a Council, but only if the Assembly first passes a resolution by a majority of its total membership AND a majority of not less than two-thirds of members present and voting. Statement 3 is wrong - Parliament is not obliged to act on the resolution; several States have passed such resolutions without a Council following. Note also that a law under Article 169 is expressly not deemed an amendment of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368.

**Q13. Answer: (c)** - *Hard* - Article 171(3): 1/3 by local authorities, 1/12 by graduates, 1/12 by teachers of at least secondary standard with three years' standing, 1/3 by MLAs from non-members, and 1/6 NOMINATED by the Governor from persons with special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art, the cooperative movement and social service. Statement 4 is therefore wrong. The arithmetic to carry: 5/6 indirectly elected, 1/6 nominated, and not a single member directly elected by the general electorate. Total strength is not more than one-third of the Assembly's strength, and not less than 40.

**Q14. Answer: (b)** - *Moderate* - Statement 2 is the key point of contrast with Parliament: there is NO joint-sitting provision for State legislatures. On an ordinary Bill the Council can delay for a maximum of about four months in total (three months on first reference plus one month on second), after which the Assembly's will simply prevails - which is why a Council is a revising chamber and not a second chamber in any real sense. Article 170 sets the Assembly at not more than 500 and not less than 60, with exceptions - Arunachal Pradesh and Goa 30, Sikkim 32, Mizoram 40.

**Q15. Answer: (d)** - *Hard* - All three are correct. Article 371A is the strongest such protection in the Constitution, covering Naga religious or social practices, Naga customary law and procedure, administration of civil and criminal justice involving decisions according to Naga customary law, and ownership and transfer of land and its resources. Article 371G gives Mizoram an almost identical protection. Article 371-J (98th Amendment, 2012) covers the Hyderabad-Karnataka region. Article 371H gives the Arunachal Governor a special responsibility for law and order, exercised in his individual judgement.

**Q16. Answer: (b)** - *Moderate* - HAM is a hybrid of EPC and BOT-Annuity: the government contributes 40% of the project cost in instalments during construction, and the remaining 60% is paid as annuities linked to a benchmark rate over the concession period. Statement 3 is wrong - under HAM the government (NHAI) collects the toll and bears the TRAFFIC risk; the concessionaire is paid its annuities irrespective of traffic. That risk split is precisely why HAM revived private participation in highways after BOT-Toll stalled.

**Q17. Answer: (c)** - *Hard* - Under EPC the government funds and owns the asset and the contractor is merely paid to build it, so no traffic risk passes to the private party. Under BOT-Toll the concessionaire finances, builds and recovers its investment from toll collection, so it carries both construction and traffic risk. Under BOT-Annuity the concessionaire carries construction risk but is paid fixed semi-annual annuities by the authority, so traffic risk stays with the government. TOT (Toll-Operate-Transfer) is different again - it monetises an already operational asset and does transfer traffic risk to the buyer.

**Q18. Answer: (c)** - *Easy* - The NaBFID Act, 2021 set up NaBFID as a development finance institution to fill the long-tenor infrastructure financing gap left after the winding down of earlier DFIs such as IDBI and IFCI. It has both developmental and financial objectives, and is regulated by the RBI as an All India Financial Institution. Related items in the same page: the Kelkar Committee (2015) on revitalising PPP and the renegotiation problem, viability gap funding, and municipal bonds.

**Q19. Answer: (a)** - *Moderate* - InvITs and REITs are regulated by SEBI under its 2014 regulations. Their whole purpose is asset recycling - transferring completed, revenue-generating assets into a trust, selling units to investors, and redeploying the proceeds. Statement 3 is wrong: InvIT units are listed and traded on stock exchanges (publicly offered InvITs must be listed), which is what gives investors an exit and makes the instrument work.

**Q20. Answer: (a)** - *Moderate* - Abolition of intermediaries - zamindari, jagirdari, inamdari - was largely accomplished in the 1950s, bringing roughly 20 million erstwhile tenants into direct relationship with the State. Tenancy reform mostly failed because tenancies were oral and unrecorded and tenants were evicted ahead of the law through 'voluntary surrenders'. Ceilings were gutted by benami transfers, partition within the family, exempted categories such as plantations, and litigation. Consolidation succeeded, but only regionally - Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh - and was barely attempted elsewhere.

**Q21. Answer: (b)** - *Moderate* - Operation Barga, launched in West Bengal from 1978, registered bargadars (sharecroppers) so that their cultivation rights became a matter of record. Its lesson is the one that matters for the exam: tenancy reform succeeded where the tenant was RECORDED, and failed where the law merely conferred a right that an unrecorded tenant could not prove. Kerala's near-complete abolition of tenancy is the other success. Option (a) describes Bhoodan; option (d) describes DILRMP.

**Q22. Answer: (c)** - *Easy* - The First Amendment Act, 1951 inserted Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule to shield zamindari abolition laws from challenge under the fundamental rights, chiefly the then Article 31 (right to property) and Article 14. Important qualification: in I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) the Supreme Court held that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule AFTER 24 April 1973 - the date of Kesavananda Bharati - are open to review for violation of the basic structure. The Ninth Schedule is therefore a shield, not an absolute one.

**Q23. Answer: (b)** - *Easy* - Vinoba Bhave began the Bhoodan (land-gift) movement in 1951 at Pochampally, in present-day Telangana, seeking voluntary donations of land for the landless. Gramdan, its later extension, sought the donation of whole villages. Morally serious and statistically marginal: a large share of the land donated was uncultivable or already under litigation, and only a fraction was ever distributed. Contrast with the modern turn from redistribution to records - DILRMP, SVAMITVA, and the NITI Aayog Model Agricultural Land Leasing Act, 2016.

**Q24. Answer: (d)** - *Easy* - The Anguttara Nikaya and the Jaina Bhagavati Sutra both list sixteen Mahajanapadas (their lists differ in detail). Statement 2 is wrong: alongside the monarchies stood the gana-sanghas or oligarchic republics - the Vajji or Licchavi confederacy at Vaishali, the Mallas, the Shakyas of Kapilavastu. Of the sixteen, four came to matter - Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti - and by the fifth century BCE the contest had narrowed to Magadha and Avanti.

**Q25. Answer: (d)** - *Moderate* - All four are standard explanations, and to them should be added timber from the same forests for building and for boats, and a succession of unsentimental and expansionist rulers. Both Mauryan-era capitals - Rajagriha, ringed by five hills, and later Pataliputra at the confluence of the Ganga and Son - were also militarily well sited. The exam favours the multi-causal answer here; single-cause options are usually the trap.

**Q26. Answer: (a)** - *Moderate* - Haryanka (Bimbisara, Ajatashatru, Udayin - who is credited with founding Pataliputra) - Shishunaga (who destroyed the power of Avanti) - Nanda (Mahapadma Nanda, described in the Puranas as the destroyer of all Kshatriyas, and the first great empire-builder of non-Kshatriya origin; the last Nanda was Dhana Nanda) - Maurya, from about 321 BCE.

**Q27. Answer: (c)** - *Hard* - The Junagadh inscription is a second-century CE record of the Western Kshatrapa (Saka) ruler Rudradaman I - not a Mauryan inscription at all. It states that the Sudarshana lake was built by Pushyagupta, a provincial governor of Chandragupta Maurya, and furnished with conduits by Tushaspha under Ashoka; Rudradaman repaired it after a breach. It is thus the best single example of an inscription of one dynasty serving as a source for another, and is also celebrated as one of the earliest long inscriptions in chaste Sanskrit.

**Q28. Answer: (d)** - *Moderate* - All four are correctly matched. The empire was administered from Pataliputra with four (later five) provinces under kumaras or princes of the blood as viceroys - Taxila for the north-west, Ujjain for the west, Suvarnagiri for the south and Tosali for Kalinga after its conquest. Below them ran the Pradeshika, the Rajukas (revenue settlement, and under Ashoka judicial authority in the countryside per Pillar Edict IV) and the Yuktas, with the Adhyakshas of the Arthashastra heading departments.

**Q29. Answer: (d)** - *Hard* - All three are correct. The Bhabru or Bairat edict (Rajasthan) is the one place where Ashoka states his Buddhist affiliation plainly and recommends specific texts to the monks - which is precisely why his Dhamma elsewhere, a civic ethic of ahimsa, respect for elders and tolerance among sects, must not be read as simple Buddhist proselytising. The Barabar caves in Bihar were dedicated to the Ajivikas by Ashoka, and the neighbouring Nagarjuni caves by his successor Dasharatha. Dhauli and Jaugada, both in Kalinga, carry the two Separate Kalinga Edicts in place of Rock Edicts XI-XIII.

**Q30. Answer: (b)** - *Moderate* - All four are correct. Brahmi, written left to right, carries the great majority of the edicts; Kharoshthi, written right to left, appears in the north-west at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra; Greek and Aramaic appear at Kandahar, at the empire's Hellenistic frontier. James Prinsep's decipherment of Brahmi in 1837 is the reason any of this is readable - and the reason the king called 'Devanampiya Piyadasi' in the edicts could later be identified with Ashoka, an identification clinched by the Maski and Gujarra minor rock edicts, which name him directly.

**Q31. Answer: (c)** - *Easy* - Rock Edict XIII records that Kalinga was conquered eight years after Ashoka's consecration - conventionally about 261 BCE - and records the remorse that followed. The edict is significantly NOT inscribed in Kalinga itself, where the two Separate Kalinga Edicts were substituted. Option (b) refers to the Chandragupta-Seleucus treaty; option (d) to the killing of the last Mauryan, Brihadratha, by Pushyamitra Shunga in about 185 BCE.

**Q32. Answer: (a)** - *Easy* - The 2016 Rules mandate three-way segregation at source into biodegradable, non-biodegradable and domestic hazardous waste, to be handed over in separate streams to authorised waste pickers or collectors. The Rules also introduced user fees, spot fines for littering, duties for bulk generators such as hotels and institutions to process biodegradable waste on their premises, and for the first time gave formal recognition to the informal waste-picker sector.

**Q33. Answer: (b)** - *Moderate* - EPR - the principle that a producer's responsibility for a product extends to its end-of-life management - entered Indian law through the E-Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011, and was subsequently extended to plastics, batteries, tyres and used oil. The plastic EPR architecture now runs on registered producers, importers and brand owners meeting annual recycling and end-of-life targets through tradable EPR certificates on the CPCB portal.

**Q34. Answer: (a)** - *Moderate* - Yellow covers human and animal anatomical waste, soiled waste, expired medicines, chemical waste and discarded linen, and goes to incineration or deep burial. Red is for contaminated recyclable waste - tubing, bottles, catheters, syringes without needles - which is autoclaved and then recycled. White (translucent) puncture-proof containers are for sharps. Blue is for broken or discarded glassware and metallic body implants.

**Q35. Answer: (c)** - *Moderate* - Indian mixed municipal waste is heavy in wet organic matter, giving it low calorific value and high moisture - the opposite of what mass-burn incineration needs - so plants either run below capacity or need auxiliary fuel, which destroys the economics and adds emissions. The corollary is the exam point: waste-to-energy is not an alternative to segregation at source but depends on it; the wet fraction belongs in composting or bio-methanation, and only the dry high-calorific fraction (RDF) is a sensible feedstock.

**Q36. Answer: (d)** - *Easy* - All three are correct. Paris replaced Kyoto's top-down, Annex-I-only binding targets with a bottom-up architecture in which every Party submits an NDC, backed by a transparency framework and a five-yearly global stocktake (the first concluded at COP28 in 2023) intended to ratchet ambition. Article 6 provides the market and non-market cooperation mechanisms. The principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities survives, but now qualified by 'in the light of different national circumstances'.

**Q37. Answer: (b)** - *Moderate* - India's updated NDC raised the emissions-intensity target from 33-35% to 45% below 2005 levels by 2030, and the non-fossil installed capacity share from 40% to about 50% by 2030. Statement 3 is wrong and is the standard trap: India's NDC is INTENSITY-based, not an absolute emissions cap, consistent with its position on CBDR-RC and its per-capita emissions. The third element of the NDC is the additional carbon sink of 2.5 to 3 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent through forest and tree cover by 2030; the long-term goal is net zero by 2070.

**Q38. Answer: (d)** - *Moderate* - All three are correct. NAPCC (2008) has eight missions - solar, enhanced energy efficiency, sustainable habitat, water, sustaining the Himalayan ecosystem, Green India, sustainable agriculture, and strategic knowledge for climate change - with State Action Plans mirroring them. The Carbon Credit Trading Scheme, notified under the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022, creates a compliance market with obligated entities and intensity targets, alongside an offset mechanism. Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment) was launched by India in 2022 and folded into the COP27 cover text.

**Q39. Answer: (b)** - *Hard* - Statements 1 and 2 are the two contrasts that matter and are the standard basis for arguing that Mauryan pillars are not simply borrowed from Persepolis. Statement 3 is plainly wrong - the animal capital is the most famous feature of the Ashokan pillar. The full anatomy runs: monolithic shaft of Chunar sandstone with the characteristic Mauryan polish, then an inverted lotus or bell-shaped member, then the abacus, then the crowning animal - lion at Sarnath and Lauriya-Nandangarh, bull at Rampurva, elephant at Sankisa.

**Q40. Answer: (c)** - *Easy* - The abacus of the Sarnath capital bears four animals in motion - lion, elephant, horse and bull - separated by four Dharmachakras. Four addorsed lions stand above; the crowning wheel, of which fragments survive, is not part of the emblem as adopted in 1950, though a Dharmachakra from the abacus was placed at the centre of the national flag. The capital was carved in Chunar sandstone with the Mauryan polish and marks the site of the Buddha's first sermon.

**Q41. Answer: (c)** - *Moderate* - Anda is the hemispherical mound, symbolically the burial mound over the relic. Harmika is the square railed balcony on its summit, from which rises the yashti bearing the chhatra or umbrella. Medhi is the raised drum or terrace on which the anda rests and which carries the upper pradakshina patha. Vedika is the railing that encloses the circumambulatory path, pierced at the cardinal points by toranas - the great carved gateways of Sanchi Stupa 1, added under the Satavahanas.

**Q42. Answer: (d)** - *Moderate* - All three are correct. The Barabar caves (Sudama, Lomas Rishi, Karna Chaupar, Vishwa Zopri) were dedicated by Ashoka and the neighbouring Nagarjuni caves by Dasharatha, in both cases to the Ajivikas - a striking fact given Ashoka's own Buddhist affiliation, and good evidence for the tolerance his Dhamma preached. The mirror-like interior polish is the Mauryan signature. The Lomas Rishi facade imitates in stone a wooden chaitya arch, and is the ancestor of the chaitya-window motif that runs through later rock-cut architecture.

**Q43. Answer: (b)** - *Easy* - The Didarganj Yakshi, found near Patna and now in the Bihar Museum, is carved in sandstone and carries the high Mauryan polish, holding a chauri or fly-whisk. It belongs to the 'popular art' strand of Mauryan sculpture - the Yaksha and Yakshi figures of Parkham, Patna and Besnagar, made for local cults - as distinct from the court art of pillars and palaces. Grey schist is the signature material of the later Gandhara school; the Mathura school used spotted red sandstone.

**Q44. Answer: (c)** - *Moderate* - The four categories are Safe (extraction up to 70% of the annually replenishable resource), Semi-critical (70-90%), Critical (90-100%) and Over-exploited (above 100%, i.e. extraction exceeding annual recharge). Over-exploited and critical units are concentrated in Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Delhi and western Uttar Pradesh, and in pockets of Tamil Nadu - the belt where assured canal or tubewell irrigation met a paddy-wheat cycle and free or heavily subsidised power.

**Q45. Answer: (a)** - *Easy* - Agriculture accounts for roughly 85-90% of water use in India, and its share of surface and groundwater use alike is overwhelming; the projected share falls only modestly by 2050 as industrial and domestic demand grow. The policy consequence follows directly: no meaningful reduction in India's water stress is possible through domestic conservation alone - it requires a change in the crop mix and in irrigation efficiency, which is why micro-irrigation and crop diversification away from paddy in the north-west are the operative levers.

**Q46. Answer: (d)** - *Easy* - Atal Bhujal Yojana, a World Bank-assisted central sector scheme of the Ministry of Jal Shakti, promotes community participation and demand-side management of groundwater in identified water-stressed blocks across seven States, with incentive funds released against measurable outcomes such as water-security plans and improved data. Option (a) describes the Jal Jeevan Mission (Har Ghar Jal). The distinction to hold: Jal Jeevan is about supply and access; Atal Bhujal is about the sustainability of the source.

**Q47. Answer: (c)** - *Hard* - All three are correct. The 4%-of-water against roughly 18%-of-population contrast is the standard opening of the NCERT chapter. Utilisable resource is far smaller than total potential because much of the monsoon flow runs off to the sea within a few weeks and cannot be stored or diverted with existing infrastructure and terrain - the gap between the two figures, not the headline total, is what defines the constraint. The north-western groundwater concentration is the direct result of the Green Revolution cropping pattern.

**Q48. Answer: (d)** - *Moderate* - All three are correct. The 1950 Treaty underpins the open border and reciprocal treatment of nationals in residence, property and trade; Nepal has long sought its revision, and an Eminent Persons Group report prepared for that purpose has never been formally received. The Kalapani-Lipulekh-Limpiyadhura tract at the Nepal-India-China trijunction was included in Nepal's revised political map of 2020. Nepal's landlocked status and transit dependence is the structural fact that makes its periodic outreach to China rational rather than merely hostile.

**Q49. Answer: (b)** - *Moderate* - The 2007 revision replaced Article 2 of the 1949 Treaty, under which Bhutan had agreed to be guided by India's advice in its external relations, with a mutual undertaking to cooperate closely and not to allow the use of their territory for activities harmful to the other's security. That single change is the whole point of the revision, and marks Bhutan's emergence as a sovereign actor in its own right. Hydropower - Chukha, Kurichhu, Tala, Mangdechhu, and the cost-overrun problem at Punatsangchhu I and II - remains the economic spine of the relationship.

**Q50. Answer: (a)** - *Hard* - Statements 1 to 3 are correct. The 100th Amendment, 2015 operationalised the 1974 Land Boundary Agreement and the exchange of enclaves and adverse possessions. The 2014 award of the Annex VII tribunal delimited the maritime boundary, and both sides accepted it - a rare and cited instance of peaceful settlement in the region. The Ganga Waters Treaty, signed on 12 December 1996 for thirty years, governs dry-season sharing at Farakka (below 70,000 cusecs the flow is shared equally) and expires on 31 December 2026; renewal discussions are under way. Statement 4 is wrong: the Teesta agreement was initialled in 2011 but has never been signed.

## Revision checklist (drill these cold)

1. **Governor, the ten articles:** 153 (a Governor per State; **7th Amendment, 1956** - one person for two or more States) - 154 executive power - 155 **appointed by the President by warrant, not elected** - 156 **pleasure of the President**, term 5 years, ***B.P. Singhal* (2010)**: not arbitrary, limited review - 157 **only two qualifications: citizen, 35** - 158 emoluments **charged on the State's CF** - 159 oath by the **Chief Justice of the High Court** - 161 pardon, **NOT for death sentence, NOT for court-martial** - 163 discretion, and **163(2) makes his own view of what is discretionary final**.
2. **Article 200, the three options** (per the Nov 2025 advisory opinion, not four): assent - reserve for the President - withhold **and return** for reconsideration. **Money Bills cannot be returned.** Reservation is **mandatory** where the Bill would derogate from the High Court's powers. A **reconsidered** Bill may still be reserved for the President.
3. **Timelines, deemed assent, justiciability - the current law.** No judicially imposed timeline; **no deemed assent**; not ordinarily justiciable; **but** prolonged unexplained inaction invites **limited** review and a bare direction to act. *State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu* (2025) is superseded on all three points.
4. **Article 213, the three cases** needing the President's prior instructions: previous sanction would have been needed for the Bill - the Governor would have reserved it - the Act would have been invalid without the President's assent. Concurrent-List subject matter is **not** one of them.
5. **Ministers, two numbers:** **164(1A)** - 15% of the **Assembly's** strength, **floor of 12** (the Union has 15% of the Lok Sabha and **no floor**). **164(1B)** - defection disqualification bars ministership. Collective responsibility runs to the **Assembly alone**.
6. **Proviso to Art 164(1) - tribal welfare minister in four States: Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha.** Bihar was in the original list and was dropped.
7. **Legislative Councils:** six States - **Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh**. **Art 169** - Parliament by **ordinary majority**, but only after an Assembly resolution by **special majority**, and **Parliament is not bound**. **Art 171** - **1/3 local bodies, 1/12 graduates, 1/12 teachers, 1/3 by MLAs from non-members, 1/6 nominated by the Governor**; total not more than **1/3 of the Assembly**, not less than **40**. **5/6 indirectly elected, 1/6 nominated, none directly elected.**
8. **Assembly and Bills:** **Art 170** - max **500**, min **60** (Arunachal and Goa 30, Sikkim 32, Mizoram 40). Council delays a **Money Bill 14 days**, an ordinary Bill about **four months in total**. **No joint sitting exists for a State legislature** - the single most-tested contrast with Parliament.
9. **Part XXI:** **371A Nagaland** (the strongest protection - Naga customary law, land and its resources, unless the Assembly resolves otherwise) - **371G Mizoram** - **371B Assam**, **371C Manipur** (Hill Areas Committee) - **371D/E Andhra Pradesh and Telangana** - **371F Sikkim** - **371H Arunachal** (Governor's special responsibility for law and order) - **371-I Goa** - **371-J Karnataka, Hyderabad-Karnataka, 98th Amendment, 2012**.
10. **PPP risk ladder, one line each:** **EPC** - government funds and owns, no traffic risk to the contractor. **BOT-Toll** - construction **and** traffic risk private. **BOT-Annuity** - construction risk private, traffic risk public. **HAM** - **40% government grant during construction, 60% as annuity, traffic risk with the government**. **TOT** - monetises an operational asset, traffic risk transfers to the buyer.
11. **Infrastructure financing:** **NaBFID Act, 2021** - **InvITs and REITs regulated by SEBI**, listed, for asset recycling - viability gap funding - municipal bonds - **Kelkar Committee (2015)** on PPP renegotiation.
12. **Land reforms, four legs:** **intermediary abolition - the one that worked**, shielded by the **First Amendment, 1951, Art 31B and the Ninth Schedule** (and note ***I.R. Coelho*, 2007**: post-24-April-1973 entries face basic-structure review). **Tenancy reform failed** except where the tenant was **recorded** - **Operation Barga, West Bengal, from 1978**, and Kerala. **Ceilings** gutted by benami transfers, family partition, exempted categories and litigation; family-based ceilings only after **1972**. **Consolidation** succeeded in Punjab, Haryana and western UP only. Then **Bhoodan - Vinoba Bhave, 1951, Pochampally** - and the modern turn from redistribution to records: **DILRMP, SVAMITVA, the NITI Aayog Model Agricultural Land Leasing Act, 2016**.
13. **Magadha to Maurya:** **sixteen Mahajanapadas**, monarchies **and** gana-sanghas (**Vajji at Vaishali**). Order: **Haryanka - Shishunaga - Nanda - Maurya**. Four provinces and capitals: **Taxila (Uttarapatha), Ujjain (Avantirashtra), Suvarnagiri (Dakshinapatha), Tosali (Kalinga)**, centre at Pataliputra; **Rajukas** with judicial authority under Pillar Edict IV.
14. **The edict corpus:** **14 Major Rock Edicts, Minor Rock Edicts, 7 Pillar Edicts**, the **two Separate Kalinga Edicts (Dhauli, Jaugada)**, the **Bhabru/Bairat edict** (Buddhist affiliation stated plainly), the **Barabar caves dedicated to the Ajivikas** (Nagarjuni by Dasharatha). Scripts: **Brahmi** mostly, **Kharoshthi** at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra, **Greek and Aramaic at Kandahar**; **Prinsep, 1837**. **Kalinga war c. 261 BCE, 8th regnal year, Rock Edict XIII** - which is *not* inscribed in Kalinga. The **Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman** is a **Saka** record and the source for the **Sudarshana lake** under Chandragupta and Ashoka.
15. **Architecture I:** Mauryan pillars are **monolithic, Chunar sandstone, Mauryan polish, sunk directly into the ground with no base** - Achaemenid pillars are **segmented and stand on bases**. **Sarnath capital**: four lions above, abacus with **lion, elephant, horse, bull** separated by wheels. Stupa: **anda** (dome) - **harmika** (railed balcony on top) - **chhatra** on the **yashti** - **medhi** (drum) - **vedika** (railing) - **torana**. **Didarganj Yakshi = polished sandstone, popular art**; Gandhara used **grey schist**, Mathura **spotted red sandstone**.
16. **Waste, rule by stream:** **SWM 2016** - three-way segregation at source (**biodegradable / non-biodegradable / domestic hazardous**). **EPR entered Indian law through the E-Waste Rules, 2011.** **BMW 2016 colours** - **yellow** anatomical and soiled, **red** contaminated recyclable plastic, **white** sharps, **blue** glassware and metallic implants. **Waste-to-energy underperforms on Indian MSW because of low calorific value and high moisture** - it depends on segregation, it does not replace it.
17. **Climate architecture:** **UNFCCC 1992 - Kyoto 1997** (Annex-I binding, CDM/JI/ET) **- Paris 2015** (bottom-up **NDCs**, five-yearly **global stocktake**, **Article 6**). **India's updated NDC (2022): 45% emissions-intensity cut from 2005 by 2030, ~50% non-fossil installed capacity by 2030, 2.5-3 bn t CO2e additional sink - intensity-based, no absolute cap.** **Net zero 2070.** **NAPCC - eight missions.** **CCTS** under the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022. **Mission LiFE.**
18. **Water:** **~4% of the world's water, ~18% of its population**; **utilisable << potential**; **agriculture takes 85-90%**; **CGWB categories - safe (<70%), semi-critical (70-90%), critical (90-100%), over-exploited (>100%)**, concentrated in Punjab, Haryana and western UP. **Jal Jeevan Mission = supply and access; Atal Bhujal Yojana = sustainability of the source.**
19. **Neighbourhood, three files:** **Nepal** - 1950 Treaty, open border, EPG report never received, **Kalapani-Lipulekh-Limpiyadhura** and the 2020 map, transit dependence. **Bhutan** - **1949 Treaty revised 2007**, the removal of the "guided by India" clause is the whole point; hydropower spine; Doklam 2017. **Bangladesh** - **LBA via the 100th Amendment, 2015**; **2014 Annex VII maritime award**; **Ganga Waters Treaty 1996, thirty years, expires 31 Dec 2026**; **Teesta initialled 2011, never signed**.
